answer: HYPOTHESIS (final answer): Within the studied window 2000–1100 BCE, the highest growth phase occurred in the 16th–15th centuries BCE, peaking in the 15th century BCE (1500–1400 BCE). Over 100-year bins, the mean archaeological growth-rate indicator g_all_mean stays near zero through the 20th–18th centuries BCE (≤0.00028, relative ranks 4–7), rises clearly in the 16th century BCE (mean 0.00115), reaches its global maximum in the 15th century BCE (0.00283, rank 1 of 10), and remains strongly positive in the 14th century BCE (0.00145, rank 2) before turning negative in the 13th century BCE (−0.00155) and bottoming out in the 12th century BCE (−0.00437). The 11th-century bin is excluded as a partial 1-year edge bin at the window boundary. The independent 100-year pollen/openness proxy pollen_grate_100 shows the same pattern: its maximum is also the 15th century BCE (0.00189, rank 1), with the 14th century BCE second (0.00111). At 50-year resolution, growth (g_all_mean) is continuously positive from ~1650 BCE through ~1350 BCE and peaks in the half-century centered on 1450 BCE (0.00298) — i.e., a sustained high-growth phase spanning the 16th–15th centuries BCE that tapers in the early 14th century BCE. Corroboration: the overall archaeological level (kde_all_mean) climbs from ~0.00025 before 1500 BCE to 0.00040–0.00043 by 1400–1300 BCE (level peaks only as the growth rate turns negative, consistent with a growth-rate peak preceding a level peak), and capital indices in the binned records cluster in/after the growth window: weapons/axes peak at 1500 BCE (ZAxtSchwert 2.95), monuments and copper/gold peak at 1400–1300 BCE (ZMonument 1.71; ZCU_AU 2.54–2.85 at 1400–1200 BCE), and hoards/deposits peak at 1100 BCE (ZHort 3.38). CONCLUSION: the highest growth phase of 2000–1100 BCE is the 16th–15th centuries BCE, with the single strongest growth century the 15th century BCE (1500–1400 BCE); growth accelerated through the 16th century BCE, peaked in the 15th, stayed positive into the early 14th, and declined through the 13th–12th centuries BCE.

payload.hypothesis: The highest growth phase of 2000-1100 BCE spans the 16th-15th centuries BCE and peaks in the 15th century BCE (1500-1400 BCE), based on the 100-year-mean growth indicator g_all_mean (max 0.00283 in the 15th century BCE, rank 1) which is independently corroborated by pollen_grate_100 (max also 15th century BCE, 0.00189), by the continuously positive 50-year growth contour from ~1650 to ~1350 BCE (peak half-century centered 1450 BCE, 0.00298), and by rising archaeological level (kde_all_mean climbing to 0.00040-0.00043 by 1400-1300 BCE) and capital-index peaks (e.g., ZAxtSchwert 2.95 in 1500 BCE, ZMonument 1.71 in 1400-1300 BCE, ZCU_AU 2.85 in 1200 BCE) concentrated in this interval; growth then turns negative in the 13th century BCE and declines through the 12th.
